title: Prevalence of Hepatitis B Virus Infection in Cameroon: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

analysis.scope_and_question: The review examines human hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection in Cameroon, focusing on the central question of estimating HBV prevalence in the general population and subpopulations using HBsAg seropositivity as the diagnostic marker.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: This is a systematic review and meta-analysis that searched Medline, Global Health, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, Africa Index Medicus, and the Journal of Health Science and Disease at the University of Yaounde. Eligible studies reported HBsAg prevalence in the general population and subpopulations, assessed using a random-effects meta-analysis with heterogeneity quantified by I2 and study quality evaluated via the Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal tool. A total of 92 papers with 100 studies were included.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The pooled overall HBV prevalence in Cameroon is 9.98% (95% CI 9.00–11.02) with high heterogeneity (I2 = 98.10%). Prevalence is higher in relatively higher-risk populations (12.70%, 95% CI 10.28–15.32) compared to relatively lower-risk populations (8.94%, 95% CI 7.84–10.11). Subgroup analyses identified sex, geographical area (regions), population risk groups, and study design as major sources of heterogeneity.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review reports substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 98.10%) that remains largely unexplained despite subgroup analyses, indicating potential unmeasured confounders or methodological inconsistencies across included studies. The high heterogeneity limits the precision of pooled estimates and complicates interpretation of regional and population-specific differences.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The findings underscore the need for targeted public health interventions, particularly for males and regions with the highest HBV prevalence, to reduce transmission and improve control measures in Cameroon. Standardized study designs and reporting across future prevalence studies are required to address heterogeneity and improve comparability.

analysis.summary_en: This systematic review and meta-analysis provides updated estimates of hepatitis B virus (HBV) prevalence in Cameroon, reporting an overall pooled prevalence of 9.98% (95% CI 9.00–11.02) with high heterogeneity (I2 = 98.10%). Prevalence is higher in higher-risk populations (12.70%) than in lower-risk populations (8.94%). Subgroup analyses indicate that sex, geographical area, population risk group, and study design are key sources of heterogeneity. The review highlights the urgent need for targeted interventions, especially among males and in high-prevalence regions, and calls for standardized methodologies in future prevalence studies to reduce heterogeneity and improve comparability.

title: Barriers to Hepatitis B Treatment: A Multicentre Cross-Sectional Registry and Survey Study by the Canadian Hepatitis B Network.

analysis.scope_and_question: Chronic hepatitis B (CHB) remains a leading cause of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) worldwide, yet treatment uptake is suboptimal even in high-resource settings. analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: A cross-sectional, retrospective analysis of 1983 adults with CHB followed in 18 Canadian hepatitis B specialty clinics between January 2018 and November 2024. An anonymous survey captured patient-reported barriers and perspectives (n = 191), while a separate survey evaluated specialist perceptions (n = 54).

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates barriers to hepatitis B treatment in Canada, focusing on treatment-eligible but untreated patients and specialist perspectives. It reveals significant disparities in treatment uptake, with younger, female, and Black/African/Caribbean patients being more likely to be untreated despite eligibility. Patient concerns include side effects, long-term therapy, and lack of curative options, while specialists highlight cost as the main barrier. The findings underscore the need for targeted interventions and policy changes to improve treatment access and outcomes for CHB patients.

title: Hepatitis B Immunity in Children on Immunomodulators: Implications From a Pediatric Dermatology Cohort and Review of the Literature

analysis.scope_and_question: The review examines hepatitis B virus (HBV) immunity in pediatric patients prior to initiating immunomodulatory therapy for dermatologic conditions, focusing on serologic testing, waning immunity, and revaccination strategies in children and young adults.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review combines a retrospective chart review of 23 pediatric and young adult patients undergoing immunomodulatory therapy with a focused literature review on HBV immunity durability, serologic interpretation, and revaccination recommendations.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Anti-HBs titers are variable and decline over time, and absence of detectable anti-HBs does not always indicate loss of immune memory or susceptibility to HBV infection.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Evidence regarding revaccination strategies is mixed, and existing guidelines derived from adult populations may not fully apply to children due to lower HBV risk and prevalence.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Guidance is needed on managing pediatric patients without serologic evidence of HBV immunity before starting biologic treatments, and screening for HBV prior to immunomodulatory therapy is recommended.

analysis.summary_en: This review evaluates HBV immunity in children and young adults before immunomodulatory therapy for dermatologic conditions. A cohort study of 23 patients found that approximately 40% lacked HBV serologic immunity. The literature review highlights that anti-HBs titers wane over time and may not reflect true immune memory. Existing adult-derived guidelines suggest screening and vaccination before therapy, but their applicability to pediatric populations remains uncertain due to lower HBV risk. Mixed evidence on revaccination strategies underscores the need for pediatric-specific guidance.

title: Attendance Among People With Hepatitis B in UK Secondary Care: A Scoping Review.

analysis.scope_and_question: The review examines non-attendance at secondary care appointments among adults with chronic hepatitis B in the UK, focusing on factors influencing appointment adherence and strategies to improve engagement within the lifelong monitoring required to prevent complications such as cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: This scoping review searched CINAHL Ultimate, Medline, Embase, Scopus and APA PsycINFO, excluded grey literature, and included 11 peer-reviewed studies examining adults with hepatitis B attending UK secondary care services; data were charted using a structured extraction form and synthesised narratively.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Non-attendance is driven by patient-related factors (e.g., limited health literacy, stigmatisation, competing priorities), system-level challenges (e.g., scheduling and accessibility), cultural or language barriers, and psychological factors such as fear of diagnosis and treatment side effects.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review does not report quantitative estimates of non-attendance rates or comparative effectiveness of interventions, and it highlights the need for co-designed, community-informed strategies to address multifactorial barriers.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Priority research includes co-designing and evaluating culturally tailored interventions with affected communities, testing reminder systems (e.g., SMS and telephone calls), and integrating community outreach into care models to improve appointment adherence.

analysis.summary_en: This scoping review synthesises evidence on non-attendance at UK secondary care appointments among adults with chronic hepatitis B, identifying multifactorial barriers including patient-related, system-level, cultural, and psychological factors. It highlights that interventions addressing these barriers—particularly culturally sensitive approaches and reminder systems—may improve engagement. The review underscores the need for co-designed, community-informed strategies and further research to evaluate their effectiveness in reducing non-attendance and supporting lifelong monitoring to prevent complications such as cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.

title: Serologic Immunity to Hepatitis A and B in US Adults and High-Risk Populations

analysis.scope_and_question: The review examines human hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection in US adults, focusing on serologic immunity prevalence and factors associated with vaccine-derived HBV immunity, specifically targeting adults aged 20 years or older and high-risk subgroups such as those with chronic liver disease, chronic kidney disease, diabetes, immunosuppression, and pregnancy (A2, A5).
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review uses a cross-sectional design with data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) from January 2017 to August 2023, including 13,514 adults with available HBV serologic test results (A3). Data were analyzed from January 3 to May 10, 2026, and weighted to generate nationally representative estimates (A4, A6). Multivariable survey-weighted logistic regression models identified independent factors associated with HBV immunity (A7).
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The review concludes that population-level serologic immunity to HBV was suboptimal, with 27.1% (95% CI, 25.8%-28.4%) demonstrating serologic immunity and 25.2% (95% CI, 23.9%-26.5%) exhibiting vaccine-derived immunity, corresponding to approximately 61.3 million and 56.9 million individuals, respectively (A9). Vaccine-derived HBV immunity was associated with younger age, female sex, non-Hispanic Asian and non-Hispanic Black race and ethnicity, and higher educational attainment (A12).
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review highlights substantial susceptibility to HBV across high-risk clinical subgroups, with vaccine-derived immunity ranging from 14.0% (95% CI, 11.3%-16.6%) in chronic kidney disease to 38.6% (95% CI, 28.0%-49.1%) in pregnancy, indicating persistent gaps in protection despite vaccination efforts (A13).
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The review emphasizes the need for targeted, systematic vaccination strategies for HBV, particularly among high-risk populations, to address suboptimal immunity and reduce susceptibility (A15).

analysis.summary_en: This review evaluates serologic immunity to hepatitis B virus (HBV) in US adults using NHANES data from 2017 to 2023. It reports that only 27.1% of adults demonstrate serologic immunity to HBV, with vaccine-derived immunity present in 25.2%, translating to approximately 61.3 million and 56.9 million individuals, respectively. Vaccine-derived immunity is more prevalent among younger adults, females, non-Hispanic Asian and Black individuals, and those with higher education. However, immunity remains suboptimal across high-risk subgroups, including chronic kidney disease (14.0%) and pregnancy (38.6%). The findings underscore persistent gaps in HBV protection and support the implementation of targeted vaccination strategies to improve immunity, particularly in high-risk populations.

title: Hepatitis B and C Prevention, Screening, and Diagnostic Services at HIV Treatment Sites: International Epidemiology Databases to Evaluate AIDS.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addressed the public-health problem that morbidity and mortality from hepatitis B virus (HBV) and hepatitis C virus (HCV) remain high among people receiving HIV care, despite the availability of effective prevention and diagnostic services. The authors identified a knowledge gap regarding the global availability of HBV and HCV services at HIV clinics.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The International epidemiology Databases to Evaluate AIDS (IeDEA) conducted a cross-sectional survey of service delivery and practices at 204 HIV treatment centers across seven global regions in 2023.
analysis.methods: The survey measured on-site availability of HBV vaccination, HBV and HCV screening, and specific tests (HBsAg, HBV DNA, HCV antibody, HCV RNA). Multivariable logistic regression models were used to test associations between site characteristics and the availability of HBV and HCV services.
analysis.main_results: HBV vaccination was available on-site at 67.7% of sites, screening for HBV and HCV at enrollment was reported by 72.1% and 50% of sites, respectively, and HBsAg, HBV DNA, HCV antibody, and HCV RNA testing were available on-site at 77%, 47.6%, 61.8%, and 44.6% of sites, respectively. Sites serving predominantly rural populations were less likely to offer on-site HBV DNA (OR 0.07; 95% CI 0.01–0.68; P=0.02), HCV antibody (OR 0.18; 95% CI 0.04–0.92; P=0.04), and HCV RNA (OR 0.10; 95% CI 0.01–0.90; P=0.04) testing.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as showing that life-saving HBV and HCV services were available on-site at most participating HIV treatment sites, but lower availability in rural settings highlights a service gap that could impede elimination efforts.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results suggest that expanding HBV and HCV services, particularly in rural areas, is critical to achieving elimination goals among people receiving HIV care.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study’s cross-sectional design and reliance on self-reported survey data limit causal inference and may overestimate service availability; the evidence strength is moderate due to potential reporting bias and limited generalizability beyond IeDEA network sites.

analysis.summary_en: This cross-sectional survey within the International epidemiology Databases to Evaluate AIDS (IeDEA) assessed the availability of hepatitis B virus (HBV) and hepatitis C virus (HCV) prevention and diagnostic services at 204 HIV treatment centers across seven global regions in 2023. The study found that HBV vaccination was available on-site at 67.7% of sites, screening for HBV and HCV at enrollment was reported by 72.1% and 50% of sites, respectively, and HBsAg, HBV DNA, HCV antibody, and HCV RNA testing were available on-site at 77%, 47.6%, 61.8%, and 44.6% of sites, respectively. Sites serving predominantly rural populations were significantly less likely to offer HBV DNA, HCV antibody, and HCV RNA testing. The authors concluded that while life-saving HBV and HCV services were available at most participating sites, lower availability in rural settings indicates a need for targeted expansion to support elimination goals among people receiving HIV care.

title: Differential Hepatitis B Surface Antigen Glycan Isomer Kinetics Between Tenofovir Alafenamide and Entecavir: Hepatocellular Carcinoma Risk Stratification in Hepatitis B e Antigen-Positive Patients.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Despite nucleos(t)ide analog therapy suppressing HBV DNA, residual hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) risk persists, creating a need for better risk-stratification markers. The study asked whether on-treatment hepatitis B surface antigen glycan isomer (HBsAgGi) kinetics could distinguish HCC risk and whether tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) outperforms entecavir (ETV) in modulating these kinetics.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This was a prospective cohort study of 90 NA-naïve chronic hepatitis B patients initiating either TAF (n=17) or ETV (n=73) and followed for 48 weeks. The population comprised HBeAg-positive and HBeAg-negative adults receiving standard-of-care antiviral therapy.
analysis.methods: HBsAgGi was quantified using a genotype C-specific O-glycosylation assay; a favourable response was defined as reduction or maintenance of low HBsAgGi levels. analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated a novel point-of-care ultrasound protocol (PUSH) for diagnosing liver disease among front-line healthcare workers in Zambia managing chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection. The authors suggest PUSH could support HBV care where laboratory and imaging resources are limited, though wide confidence intervals and a small training cohort constrain precision.

analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The retrospective design, modest sample size (n=130), and single-centre setting limit generalisability and may introduce selection bias; the evidence is assessed as moderate due to these constraints and the absence of external validation.

title: Clinically Relevant Risk of Hepatitis B Virus Infection and Reactivation in People with HIV After Withdrawal of Anti-HBV–Active Antiretroviral Therapy in Japan

analysis.study_design_and_population: This retrospective study enrolled 141 CHB patients with advanced hepatic fibrosis/compensated cirrhosis who received tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), with patients allocated into LLV and complete virological response (CVR) groups based on HBV DNA levels at week 48.
analysis.methods: Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analysis were carried out to determine risk factors for LLV development, with LLV defined as HBV DNA levels of 20-2000 IU/mL and CVR as HBV DNA levels below 20 IU/mL.

Among 141 patients, 17.0% developed LLV, defined as HBV DNA levels of 20-2000 IU/mL at week 48. The multivariate analysis confirmed this baseline viral load as strongly associated with LLV (OR = 18.824, P = 0.019). This finding provides a valuable prognostic indicator for clinicians managing high-risk CHB patients, potentially enabling earlier intervention to prevent disease progression and complications like hepatocellular carcinoma.
